articles.title: ‘Sad lost souls’: Taika Waititi lambasts critics after Klara and the Sun box-office disaster
articles.summary: The Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higher.
body: Taika Waititi has launched a furious broadside at “critics” following the disastrous commercial performance of Klara and the Sun, his new film adapted from a Kazuo Ishiguro novel.
In a post on social media, Waititi wrote: “This Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics.”
He added: “The same people who also hated Jojo Rabbit … Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”

Pointing to the disparity of the film’s audience and critics’ score on review aggregator site Rotten Tomatoes, which currently stands at 74% for the former and 26% (from 90 reviews) for the latter, Waititi also wrote: “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people.”

articles.title: Blockhead review – struggling novelist embraces his inner monster in comic thriller of literary machismo
articles.summary: Writer-director Matt Harlock looks into ego and insecurity in a smart film about a BritLit bad boy who goes down a grisly road. This has nothing to do with Ian Dury; rather, it is a brisk, effective British indie thriller informed by the legend of Robert Louis Stevenson wrestling his shadow self…
body: No prizes, then, for guessing which David Fincher film provides the template here. Typing to a soundtrack of his own best reviews (“The world needs to hear your story”), an emboldened Will is soon exploring grislier avenues, including home invasion and murder, while his increasingly unhinged rants to creative-writing students attract a rapt protege. Evoking a world where publishers push books with unequivocally positive pull quotes like “confrontational” and “dangerous”, Harlock is taking a red pencil to hackneyed notions of bad-boy writers. There is, he posits, only so much muscle one can wield while hunched over a laptop.

articles.title: ‘We both know how we feel about death and dying’: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney on their brutally honest Parkinson’s drama
articles.summary: Written by Vicar of Dibley co-creator Paul Mayhew-Archer, who has the disease, Onwards and Sideways sees the actors play a couple who bond over their diagnoses – a devastating subject but laced with humour too, they say.
body: A head of production on their first job together, Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney didn’t undergo the standard “chemistry read” to make sure they got on. Which is remarkable, given what their characters would have to do to each other in Onwards and Sideways.

In the Norfolk-set BBC film directed by John Madden (Shakespeare in Love), Ifans would have to nearly throttle Linney while in the grip of night terrors, she’d have to collapse in his arms in a weeping mess having bankrupted herself with a gambling addiction; both situations arising from the neurological condition afflicting their characters: Parkinson’s disease.

But despite being thrown into the deep end in this hugely emotional, often hilarious film, both actors acknowledge an immediate feeling of safety around each other as they embarked on a project that would require them to strip themselves bare. “It’s odd,” says Ifans, “you learn so much about each other so quickly. I couldn’t tell you what kind of car Laura drives. What her home looks like. But we both know how we feel about death and dying.”

articles.title: I Died review – moving portrait of Tzotzil women confronting patriarchal violence in the Mexican highlands
articles.summary: Ana Ts’uyeb’s poetic film celebrates the resilience of Indigenous women while exploring the possibility of a different future. Shot in her home village of Naranjatic Alto in the Mexican highlands, Ana Ts’uyeb’s documentary debut is a stirring ode to the courageous women of the Indigenous Tzotzil…
body: The patterns of systemic abuse and disenfranchisement are startlingly similar. All three women recall past opportunities to advance their education, hopes and dreams that were squashed by fathers and other male relatives. Also rampant are physical and psychological abuse. There’s a sobering matter-of-fact tone to their reminiscence; their unfortunate experiences appear to be a common reality endured by many Tzotzil women.

In place of conventional sit-down interviews, Ts’uyeb dynamically captures her subjects at work, lending a dose of cinematic poetry to everyday rituals. From weaving cloth and sieving grain to the back-breaking toil of harvest, these diaristic vignettes not only speak to a collective resilience but also act as a visual archive of Indigenous customs and traditions. Previously exploited for their labour but excluded from land inheritance, these brave women can now pour their blood, sweat and tears into their own land, thanks to the Zapatista movement.
points: Ana Ts’uyeb’s poetic film celebrates the resilience of Indigenous women while exploring the possibility of a different future.

articles.title: Ukraine-Set Drama About a Trans Man Barred From Fleeing War, ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,’ Wins Tokyo’s Ethical Film Award
articles.summary: German director and screenwriter Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” has won the Tokyo International Film Festival’s Ethical Film Award. The award, set up in 2023 with sponsor Sumitomo Corporation, highlights films that shed light on issues such as the environment, poverty and…
body: Actor Isomura Hayato, a two-time Japan Academy Film Prize winner who runs the Shizuoka Film Festival in his hometown, headed this year’s jury. He was joined by three members of the festival’s student PR team. The other nominees were Brazil’s “Amadeo and the Hypothetical New World,” directed by Brenda Lígia and Edu Felistoque, and Australia’s “Time and Tide,” directed by Vee Shi.

Stever’s film, a Germany-Ukraine co-production, opens in Kyiv at the end of 2021, months before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Oleh, a trans man, tries to leave the country to escape the coming war but is barred because of the gender listed on his documents. He stays behind with his partner, Olya, and the couple struggle to hold on to their relationship and their sense of self as the bombing draws closer.

Stever’s earlier films have had their premieres at the Berlinale and at festivals in Toronto, Locarno and Busan. She worked on her two most recent features with her wife, the Ukrainian novelist and screenwriter Anna Melikova.

body: “ Harry Potter ” agent The Blair Partnership has appointed Will Obbard and Alex Flanagan to senior roles as the company eyes a new phase of growth.

Obbard joins from theme park operator Merlin Entertainments, where he was VP of partnerships. He will lead TBP’s five-year growth strategy focusing on new revenue streams via partnerships, new franchises, mergers and acquisitions. He will also seek out new revenue opportunities for existing clients and IP.
Obbard spent over 12 years at Merlin and before that worked in strategy and M&A at KPMG.

“I’m thrilled to be joining The Blair Partnership at such an exciting point in its development,” said Obbard, who is an official World Book Day trustee. “The group has an exceptional portfolio of clients and intellectual property, alongside significant opportunities to build new partnerships and revenue streams. I’m looking forward to working with the team to deliver on its ambitious growth strategy.”

articles.title: ‘The Debut’ to Open Marrakech Film Festival, With ‘Artificial’ and ‘Paper Tiger’ Among Gala Screenings
articles.summary: Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” starring Julianne Moore as a shy housewife who is cast in a community theater musical and transforms into a zealous Method actor, has been set as the opening film of the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival.
body: Eisenberg and Moore are both expected to be on hand for the out-of-competition gala.

Other Marrakech gala screenings include two world premieres: Brazilian director Fellipe Barbosa’s “Leila et la nuit,” inspired by the life of Moroccan photographer Leila Alaoui and starring Roschdy Zem and Marina Foïs; and Egyptian helmer Omar Hilal’s “His Weakest Creatures,” which pairs Egyptian stars Ahmed Helmy and Hend Sabry together on screen for the first time.

John Turturro will be making the trek to present Noah Segan’s “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” in which the actor delivers a standout performance as an aging pickpocket contending with the contemporary world. The section also includes Laïla Marrakchi’s “Strawberries,” which has been selected as Morocco’s Oscars entry and follows a group of Moroccan seasonal laborers hired to pick strawberries in Spain who decide to stand up to their abusive employers.
The Official Competition showcases new talent in world cinema with 14 first and second feature films competing for the Étoile d’Or, awarded by a jury headed by actor Marion Cotillard.

articles.title: Palestinian-Jordanian Filmmaker Darin J. Sallam on the Backlash to ‘Farha’: ‘I Never Regretted It’
articles.summary: Sallam has no regrets about making “Farha,” her debut feature about a Palestinian girl coming of age during the Nakba, the mass displacement and dispossession of Palestinians surrounding the creation of the state of Israel in 1948.
body: “Farha” was inspired by the story of a Palestinian refugee, passed down to Sallam through her mother. The film premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in 2021, was later selected as Jordan’s submission for the international feature Oscar and subsequently streamed globally on Netflix.

Its Netflix release prompted a fierce backlash, particularly over a scene depicting Israeli soldiers killing a Palestinian family. Israeli officials publicly condemned the film, while Sallam and others involved with it faced harassment and online abuse. Sallam has also been unable to travel to Palestine since the film’s release.

The warnings rolled in even before the film was shot. “I always knew in my heart that choosing ‘Farha’ as my debut feature film would be an experience unlike anything I had encountered before or will encounter in the future,” she says.

For Sallam, the film grew out of a broader conviction that history is most powerful when experienced through individual lives. “Personal stories are often the most powerful way to understand history and society,” she explains. “Behind every historical event, there are individual lives, emotions, struggles and dreams that deserve to be heard.”

articles.title: Martha Stewart says she 'really screwed up' with homeless Halloween costume
articles.summary: The veteran lifestyle guru has deleted a photo of herself wearing torn clothes and dirt on her face.
body: Veteran lifestyle guru Martha Stewart has admitted she "really screwed up" by dressing as a homeless person for Halloween.

She posted a statement on Sunday saying she was "distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention".

That was followed by a fuller apology. "It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up. My earlier statement didn't go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry."
Stewart had captioned her original Instagram photo: "My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!"

articles.title: Jack Lowden Is Tight-Lipped on Those Bond Rumors: “I’m Not Going to Add to the Noise”
articles.summary: The 'Slow Horses' star, who is next set to play Mr. Darcy in Netflix's 'Pride and Prejudice' adaptation, admitted the speculation is "very flattering."
body: Jack Lowden isn’t giving anything away on his rumored screen tests for the role of James Bond.

In an interview with British GQ published on Monday, the Scottish star briefly touches on the reports — including those from The Hollywood Reporter — that he is part of a small group of actors eyed for the next incarnation of Ian Fleming’s beloved spy, next to Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor.

“It’s all very flattering,” says Lowden, who proceeded to pour “cold water” on the topic, according to British GQ ‘s Kieran Morris. “It’s nice to be mentioned — for any role — and I’m just not really going to add to the noise,” he continues. “It’s very nice, and Gary’s a sweetheart. It’s particularly lovely, coming from someone like him. But I don’t really listen to it.”

articles.title: The One Problem With Star Wars, According To Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir [Exclusive]
articles.summary: Everyone has an opinion about Star Wars, including Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir, who has some general ideas about what the franchise needs.
body: You can count "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary" author Andy Weir among those with some thoughts on the matter. The novelist has already enjoyed a big 2026 to this point, beginning with Phil Lord and Chris Miller's blockbuster adaptation of "Project Hail Mary." As he's gearing up to release another passion project of his, the upcoming Audible original sci-fi series "Exoplanet" that he's executive producing, I had the opportunity to speak with Weir over Zoom. During our extended conversation, the topic of "Star Wars" came up and, unsurprisingly, Weir had plenty to say.

"'Star Wars' is more about massive upheaval. One problem that happens is, if you're going to have a story about a monumental war, then when it's over and the good guys win, you want it to stay that way. So it's very unsatisfying if you roll into a new monumental war."
